settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: validateCrumb uses MessageDigest.isEqual for constant-time comparison (lines 99-101)
When md is null or request is not HttpServletRequest, issueCrumb returns null and validateCrumb returns false (lines 72, 86-88, 96-104), i.e. no open-fail path
The crumb still incorporates the authentication principal name from Jenkins.getAuthentication() (lines 75-78)
candidates.description: DefaultCrumbIssuer constructs its MessageDigest as MD5 and issues crumbs by hashing the authenticated principal name and client IP together with a salt. validateCrumb compares values via MessageDigest.isEqual (constant-time). The crumb is only a function of (user name, client IP when not excluded, salt); when 'excludeClientIPFromCrumb' is enabled the crumb no longer binds to the client address, so any value that leaks or can be recomputed for the target user (with a known salt) is reusable from other hosts. Additionally, issueCrumb returns null when the request is not an HttpServletRequest and the digest was unavailable (readResolve leaves md null on NoSuchAlgorithmException), and validateCrumb then returns false, i.e. failures are closed rather than open. This is a weakness/design observation about the default crumb algorithm rather than a demonstrated bypass; no exploitation path is verified in source.
missing_evidence: Whether any deployment commonly enables excludeClientIPFromCrumb and how salt is provisioned/rotated
An end-to-end request path where a recomputed/replayed crumb is accepted for a different origin
Whether MD5 collision/truncation is exploitable for crumb forgery in practice
preconditions: excludeClientIPFromCrumb set to true (reduces binding to the client address)
Attacker can obtain a valid crumb for the victim identity and reaches the POST endpoint
candidates.title: Crumb validation depends on MD5-based DefaultCrumbIssuer and returns null issueCrumb for non-HttpServletRequest

counter_evidence: The crumb still mixes the authenticated user name, so a value valid for the victim identity is also required (lines 75-78)
When a trusted proxy sets X-Forwarded-For itself, the header value is not attacker-controlled
candidates.description: DefaultCrumbIssuer.getClientIP reads the X-Forwarded-For request header and, when present, splits it on comma and uses the first element as the client IP incorporated into the crumb. The header is fully attacker-controlled unless a trusted reverse proxy overwrites it. This means the client-IP component of the crumb can be chosen by the requester, which weakens (and, when combined with excludeClientIPFromCrumb handling, potentially negates) the address binding of the crumb. The code does not validate the header value nor restrict it to a configured set of trusted proxies.
missing_evidence: Whether any core code path or configuration validates/overwrites X-Forwarded-For before it reaches this method
A concrete request sequence demonstrating crumb reuse across origins due to the spoofable header
preconditions: CSRF protection enabled with DefaultCrumbIssuer and excludeClientIPFromCrumb false
Jenkins reachable behind a proxy/network where the client can set X-Forwarded-For
Attacker can observe or predict the crumb value for the chosen forged IP
candidates.title: Client IP used in crumb taken from untrusted X-Forwarded-For header

counter_evidence: BlacklistedTypesConverter registered at PRIORITY_VERY_HIGH (SECURITY-247 defense, line 163)
DynamicProxyConverter overridden to throw on unmarshal (SECURITY-105 defense, lines 165-172)
RobustReflectionConverter used instead of default reflection converter (line 125)
candidates.description: XStream2.wrapMapper calls AnnotationMapper.autodetectAnnotations(true) and the in-source comment explicitly notes this is unsafe (JENKINS-19561). XStream2 is the deserialization layer for XML configuration in this code base. Although a BlacklistedTypesConverter (SECURITY-247 defense) and a dynamic-proxy-rejecting DynamicProxyConverter (SECURITY-105 defense) are registered, annotation autodetection in combination with XStream's reflection-based converter has historically widened the gadget surface for attacker-influenced XML. The presence of the safeguards is counter-evidence, but the unsafe autodetect setting remains enabled.
missing_evidence: The concrete contents of the ClassFilter/XStream blacklist used at this revision
An end-to-end untrusted input path to XStream2.unmarshal in this snapshot
Whether autodetectAnnotations(true) is actually exploitable given the registered converters
preconditions: Attacker can supply XML that reaches an XStream2-based unmarshal (e.g., configuration or data files under attacker influence)
A usable gadget class reachable through XStream conversion passes the registered blacklist/denylist checks
candidates.title: XStream2 unmarshalling enables annotation autodetection (JENKINS-19561 flagged unsafe in source)
